newsitem.title: GERMANY: German asset managers use football as crowd-puller.
newsitem.headline: German asset managers use football as crowd-puller.

text.p: German investment and asset managers, like the breweries before them, are gradually discovering the pulling-power of football and its heroes in attracting hitherto untapped audiences for their products.

Signing an advertising deal with German national soccer star Oliver Bierhoff on Thursday, top German bank Deutsche Bank AG said it now saw "The Beautiful Game" as one of the most direct routes through to the small investor.
"Through football, we can reach the masses -- people who can perhaps only afford to save 100 marks a month,' said Joerg-Matthias Butzlaff at Deutsche's asset management subsidiary DWS.

Bierhoff, who shot to stardom in Germany after scoring the "Golden Goal" against the Czech republic in the final of the last European Championships in England, plays abroad in Italy for Udinese Calcio.
But such is his popularity that DWS will be using Bierhoff for a wide print and television advertising campaign for their long-term savings product "Investmentrente".
German breweries have long used the sport as a vehicle for advertising, whether through television commercials or placards placed in the stadium.
But DWS's rival DIT asset managers, a subsidiary of Dresdner Bank AG was something of a pioneer in the financial services sector when it started advertising at soccer games early last year.
"We departed from the traditional approach to try and boost awareness levels for our products," DIT's Thomas Kalich said.

The strategy appears to have worked, with DIT saying it has registered between 2,000 and 3,000 interested callers for its "Vorsorgeplan" pension scheme directly after each of the 12 international matches at which it has placed placards.
Kahlich said the savings bank now planned to expand its football-based advertising through 1997.
Germany, with its highly-developed television and print media, is one of Europe's largest advertising markets.

Figures released in a study by advertising sellers IP Deutschland earlier this week showed TV advertising revenues last year stood at around seven billion marks, with newspaper and other print media pulling in a total 14.5 billion.
